title: Instant Pot Cuban-Style Ropa Vieja with Yellow Rice & Plantains
dek: Pressure-braised chuck shreds into a savory tomato, pepper and olive sauce while yellow rice and caramelized plantains turn it into a complete family platter.
image_alt: Cuban-style shredded beef in tomato sauce served with yellow rice and caramelized plantains
ingredients: 3 lb boneless beef chuck roast, cut into 3 equal pieces
1 green bell pepper, seeded and cut into 1/2-inch strips
1 red bell pepper, seeded and cut into 1/2-inch strips
1/2 cup pimiento-stuffed green olives, drained and halved
2 ripe plantains with mostly black skins, peeled and cut on the bias into 1/2-inch slices
2 tbsp neutral oil, for the plantains
2 tbsp chopped cilantro or flat-leaf parsley
Hot sauce or sliced pickled chiles, optional for serving

instructions.name: Season and brown the beef
instructions.text: Pat the chuck dry and season with 1 1/2 teaspoons salt and the black pepper. Select Sauté on High on a 6-quart electric pressure cooker, add 1 tablespoon oil and brown the beef in two batches for about 3 minutes per broad side. Transfer to a plate.

instructions.name: Sauté the vegetables
instructions.text: Add the onion and both bell peppers to the pot. Cook for 4 minutes, stirring and scraping, until slightly softened. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds. Remove half of the pepper mixture to a bowl so it keeps some texture for the finished sauce.

instructions.name: Deglaze and layer
instructions.text: Cancel Sauté. Pour 1 cup broth into the pot and scrape until no browned bits remain. Return the beef and its juices. Sprinkle on the cumin, oregano and paprika and add the bay leaves. Whisk the crushed tomatoes, tomato paste and remaining 1/2 cup broth, then pour over the beef without stirring it into the base. Keep the contents below the maximum-fill line.

instructions.name: Pressure cook and release
instructions.text: Lock the lid and cook on High Pressure for 50 minutes; allow about 15 minutes for the cooker to reach pressure. Let pressure release naturally for 15 minutes, then vent the remainder in short controlled pulses with hands and face away from steam. Stop if liquid sputters and open only after the float valve drops.

instructions.name: Cook the yellow rice
instructions.text: While the beef cooks, combine the rinsed rice, 3 cups water, turmeric and remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt in a saucepan. Bring to a boil, cover, reduce to low and cook for 15 minutes. Remove from heat, rest covered for 10 minutes and fluff.

instructions.name: Shred and finish the sauce
instructions.text: Transfer the beef to a board and discard the bay leaves. Check the center: beef is safe at 145°F with a 3-minute rest, but chuck should reach about 195 to 205°F and pull apart easily for this dish. Shred with two forks. Select Sauté on High and simmer the sauce for 8 to 10 minutes with the reserved peppers, olives and olive brine. Stir in the vinegar, return the beef and cook 2 minutes more. Cancel Sauté.

instructions.name: Caramelize the plantains and serve
instructions.text: Heat 2 tablespoons oil in a large skillet over medium. Fry the plantains in a single layer for 2 to 3 minutes per side, until deep golden and tender; work in batches if needed. Serve the ropa vieja with yellow rice and plantains, sprinkle with herbs and offer heat at the table.

why_it_works: Thin broth sits directly on a completely deglazed base while the tomato mixture stays on top, reducing burn-warning risk from tomato solids.
Chuck roast has enough collagen to become succulent after a 50-minute pressure cycle and staged release, unlike lean flank steak, which can dry out.
Reserving half the peppers and reducing the sauce after pressure restores fresh texture and concentrates flavor without thickening the liquid before pressurizing.
swaps: Use a 3 lb brisket flat trimmed to a 1/4-inch fat cap; keep the 50-minute pressure time and test for easy shredding before proceeding.
For a lighter side, replace the fried plantains with roasted sweet plantains brushed with 1 tablespoon oil and baked at 425°F for 18 to 22 minutes.
Use plain green olives plus 1 tablespoon capers if pimiento-stuffed olives are unavailable; taste before adding extra salt.
storage: Cool the beef and sides in separate shallow containers within 2 hours. Refrigerate the ropa vieja and rice for up to 4 days and the plantains for up to 3 days. Reheat beef and rice with a splash of broth until they reach 165°F; re-crisp plantains in a 375°F oven or air fryer. Freeze the beef in sauce for up to 3 months, but freeze rice and plantains separately.
notes: Total time includes browning, approximately 15 minutes to pressurize, the 50-minute cook, a 15-minute natural release and sauce reduction; rice and plantains cook during those stages.
The shared sauce is intentionally mild. Put hot sauce, pickled chiles or crushed red pepper on the table for diners who want heat.
Written for a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Follow the minimum-liquid, maximum-fill and venting instructions for your exact model and never force the lid.
If the beef resists shredding, return it to at least 1 cup of thin sauce, cook on High Pressure for 8 minutes and allow a 10-minute natural release.
Very ripe plantains should have mostly black skins; yellow plantains with green tips remain starchy and will not caramelize as softly.

faqs.q: Can I skip browning the beef?
faqs.a: Yes, but the sauce will taste less developed. If you skip it, still sauté the vegetables, add the broth and scrape the base before layering in the beef and tomato mixture.

faqs.q: Why did my cooker show a burn warning?
faqs.a: Tomato paste or crushed tomatoes probably reached the hot base, or browned bits remained after sautéing. Move the contents to a bowl, clean the base, add at least 1 1/2 cups thin broth and return the food with tomato solids on top.

faqs.q: Can I make ropa vieja ahead?
faqs.a: Yes. The beef improves after a night in its sauce. Chill promptly, remove any hardened fat and reheat gently to 165°F while you make fresh rice and plantains.

title: Instant Pot Ukrainian-Style Beet Borscht with White Beans & Dill
dek: Ruby beets, potatoes, carrots and tender white beans make a bright meatless pressure-cooker soup finished with cabbage, dill and a clean vinegar tang.
image_alt: Ruby beet soup with white beans, potatoes, carrots and vegetables in a white bowl
ingredients: 1 tbsp sunflower oil or olive oil
2 medium carrots, peeled and cut into 1/2-inch pieces
1 1/2 lb red beets, peeled and cut into 1/2-inch cubes
12 oz Yukon Gold potatoes, cut into 3/4-inch cubes
2 cans (15 oz each) cannellini beans, rinsed and drained
3 tbsp red wine vinegar, plus more to taste
1/3 cup chopped fresh dill, plus more for serving
3/4 cup sour cream or plain Greek yogurt, optional for serving
Prepared horseradish or hot sauce, optional for serving

instructions.name: Sauté the aromatics
instructions.text: Select Sauté on a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Add the oil, onion and carrots and cook for 4 minutes, stirring, until the onion softens. Add the garlic and cook 30 seconds. Cancel Sauté.

instructions.name: Deglaze and layer
instructions.text: Pour in the broth and water and scrape the base until completely clean. Add the beets, potatoes, bay leaves, 1 teaspoon salt and black pepper. Spoon the diced tomatoes and tomato paste over the vegetables without stirring them into the base. Keep the contents below the model's maximum-fill line.

instructions.name: Pressure cook and release
instructions.text: Lock the lid and cook on High Pressure for 6 minutes; allow about 12 to 15 minutes to reach pressure. Let pressure release naturally for 10 minutes, then vent the remainder in short controlled pulses with hands and face away from steam. Pause if liquid sputters and open only after the float valve drops.

instructions.name: Finish the cabbage and beans
instructions.text: Discard the bay leaves. Select Sauté on Low and stir in the cabbage, beans, vinegar, sugar and remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt. Simmer uncovered for 5 to 7 minutes, until the cabbage is tender but not limp and the beans are hot.

instructions.name: Balance and serve
instructions.text: Cancel Sauté and stir in the dill. Taste and add vinegar for brightness, salt for savoriness or a pinch more sugar only if the beets need balance. Ladle into bowls and serve with sour cream and bread; offer horseradish or hot sauce at the table.

why_it_works: Beets and potatoes pressure-cook in ample thin broth, while tomato solids stay on top of the clean base to reduce burn-warning risk.
Canned beans and cabbage go in after pressure, so the beans stay intact and the cabbage retains texture instead of turning sulfurous and soft.
Vinegar added after pressure preserves its bright acidity and balances the natural sweetness of beets, carrots and tomatoes.
swaps: Use drained navy beans or great northern beans in place of cannellini beans; add them only after pressure as written.
For a dairy-free bowl, use unsweetened plant-based yogurt or omit the creamy garnish entirely.
Golden beets work with the same timing, though the finished soup will be amber rather than ruby.
storage: Cool in shallow containers within 2 hours and refrigerate for up to 5 days. Reheat on the stovetop or in the microwave until the soup reaches 165°F, adding a splash of broth if it thickens. Freeze without sour cream for up to 3 months; thaw overnight and add fresh dill after reheating.
notes: Total time includes about 12 to 15 minutes to pressurize, the 6-minute cycle, a 10-minute natural release and the final cabbage simmer.
Beet juice stains porous surfaces. Use a washable cutting board and rinse the cooker lid and silicone ring soon after cooking.
The base is family-mild; horseradish, hot sauce and extra black pepper belong at the table.
Written for a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Follow your model manual's minimum-liquid, fill-limit and venting rules and never force the lid.
Do not substitute dry beans at the same timing. Dry beans need a separate, longer pressure cycle and must remain below the half-full line because they expand and foam.

faqs.q: Can I grate the beets instead of cubing them?
faqs.a: Yes. Coarsely grated beets cook faster and will nearly dissolve, making a more uniform broth. Keep the programmed time the same so the potatoes still become tender.

faqs.q: Why is my borscht brown instead of bright red?
faqs.a: Older beets, prolonged boiling and too little acid can dull the color. Add the vinegar only after pressure, avoid a long hard simmer and taste for a pleasantly bright finish.

faqs.q: Does borscht taste better the next day?
faqs.a: Yes. A chilled overnight rest melds the earthy, sweet and sour notes. Reheat only what you need to 165°F and add fresh dill and sour cream after heating.

title: Mexican Chiles en Nogada with Pork-Fruit Picadillo & Walnut Sauce
dek: Roasted poblanos cradle a warmly spiced pork-and-fruit filling beneath cool walnut cream, pomegranate and parsley for a striking seasonal centerpiece.
image_alt: Roasted poblano stuffed with pork-fruit picadillo and covered in walnut cream, pomegranate seeds and parsley
ingredients: 1 cup whole milk, plus more as needed
1 small tart apple, peeled, cored and cut into 1/4-inch dice
1 firm-ripe pear, peeled, cored and cut into 1/4-inch dice
1 small peach, peeled, pitted and cut into 1/4-inch dice, or 1/2 cup thawed frozen peach
1/2 cup Mexican crema or sour cream
2 tbsp dry sherry or apple juice

instructions.name: Soak the walnuts
instructions.text: Cover the walnuts with 1 cup milk and soak for at least 30 minutes while preparing the peppers and filling. Drain, reserving 1/2 cup soaking milk.

instructions.name: Roast and peel the poblanos
instructions.text: Heat the broiler with a rack 5 inches from the element. Broil the poblanos on a foil-lined rimmed sheet pan for 8 to 12 minutes, turning, until blistered and blackened all over. Cover in a bowl for 10 minutes, then peel gently. Cut one lengthwise slit in each, leaving the stem attached, and remove the seeds and membranes.

instructions.name: Build the picadillo
instructions.text: Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium. Cook the onion for 4 minutes, then add the garlic for 30 seconds. Add the pork, 1 teaspoon salt, black pepper, cinnamon, cloves and allspice. Cook 7 to 9 minutes, breaking it into small crumbles, until no pink remains and the center reaches 160°F.

instructions.name: Add fruit and concentrate
instructions.text: Stir in the crushed tomatoes, apple, pear, peach and raisins. Simmer for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring often, until the fruit is tender and the mixture is moist but not wet. Fold in the almonds, taste and add the remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt if needed. Cool for 10 minutes.

instructions.name: Blend the walnut sauce
instructions.text: Blend the drained walnuts, cream cheese, crema, sherry, sugar, 1/8 teaspoon cinnamon and 1/4 cup reserved milk until smooth. Add more reserved milk 1 tablespoon at a time to make a thick, pourable sauce. Refrigerate while filling the chiles.

instructions.name: Fill and warm the chiles
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 350°F. Set the poblanos in a lightly oiled baking dish, divide the picadillo among them and gently close the sides over the filling. Cover loosely with foil and bake for 12 to 15 minutes, until the centers reach 165°F.

instructions.name: Sauce and garnish
instructions.text: Let the stuffed chiles stand for 5 minutes. Spoon the cool walnut sauce generously over each warm chile and scatter with pomegranate arils and parsley. Serve promptly so the warm filling and cool sauce remain distinct.

why_it_works: Broiling blisters the poblanos for easy peeling while leaving them sturdy enough to hold a generous filling.
Cooking the pork to 160°F before adding fruit removes raw-meat guesswork, and reducing the picadillo prevents watery stuffed peppers.
Milk-soaked walnuts blend into a pale, creamy sauce whose cool richness balances the warm spices, fruit and poblano.
swaps: Use ground turkey instead of pork and cook it to 165°F; add 1 tablespoon olive oil if the turkey is very lean.
When peaches are out of season, use thawed frozen peach or a well-drained canned peach packed in juice.
For an alcohol-free sauce, replace dry sherry with unsweetened apple juice or additional milk plus 1 teaspoon lemon juice.
storage: Store stuffed chiles and walnut sauce separately in covered containers for up to 3 days. Reheat the chiles, covered, in a 325°F oven until the centers reach 165°F, then add cold sauce and fresh garnish. Freeze the filled chiles without sauce for up to 1 month; the walnut sauce does not freeze smoothly.
notes: Total time includes the walnut soak, pepper steaming and a short cooling period for the filling.
Wear gloves if poblanos irritate your skin, and avoid touching your eyes while removing seeds and membranes.
Poblanos vary in heat. This version removes all seeds and membranes; serve sliced chile or hot sauce separately.
Use only fresh-smelling walnuts. Rancid nuts make the sauce bitter and cannot be rescued by extra sugar.
Ground pork must reach 160°F; assembled stuffed chiles should be reheated to 165°F before serving.

faqs.q: Are chiles en nogada served hot or cold?
faqs.a: The filled poblanos are best warm, while the walnut sauce is cool or at room temperature. That contrast keeps the sauce fresh-tasting and the pork filling comforting.

faqs.q: Can I peel poblanos a day ahead?
faqs.a: Yes. Refrigerate the peeled, seeded poblanos in a covered container for up to 24 hours. Blot away collected moisture before filling so the picadillo stays concentrated.

faqs.q: Why is my walnut sauce gray?
faqs.a: Walnut skins and oxidation can darken it. Choose pale fresh walnuts, soak them, blend just before chilling and keep the sauce covered. The color does not affect safety.

title: Burmese-Style Tea Leaf Salad with Cabbage, Peanuts & Dried Shrimp
dek: Fermented tea leaves, crisp cabbage, tomatoes, peanuts, toasted seeds and savory dried shrimp make a punchy, many-textured salad in 30 minutes.
image_alt: Burmese-style tea leaf salad with shredded cabbage, tomatoes, peanuts, seeds and dried shrimp on a white plate
ingredients: 1/3 cup roasted split peas or roasted chickpeas
1/3 cup dried shrimp, rinsed and patted dry
1/2 small green cabbage, very thinly sliced (about 5 cups)
2 medium plum tomatoes, seeded and cut into 1/2-inch pieces
1/2 small red onion, very thinly sliced
1/2 cup mung bean sprouts, blanched in boiling water for 1 minute, cooled and thoroughly dried
1/2 cup prepared fermented tea leaf dressing (lahpet), well stirred
1 tbsp fish sauce, plus more to taste
1/4 tsp kosher salt, only if needed
1 small fresh chile, thinly sliced, optional for serving
4 cups hot cooked jasmine rice, optional for making a full meal

instructions.name: Make crisp garlic oil
instructions.text: Combine the oil and sliced garlic in a small skillet over medium-low heat. Cook for 5 to 7 minutes, stirring often, until the garlic is pale gold. Immediately strain through a fine-mesh strainer into a heat-safe bowl; spread the garlic on a paper towel. Reserve 3 tablespoons garlic oil and cool.

instructions.name: Toast the crunchy mix
instructions.text: Wipe out the skillet. Add the peanuts, split peas and sesame seeds and toast over medium heat for 2 minutes, stirring, until fragrant. Add the dried shrimp and toast for 1 minute more. Transfer to a plate to cool.

instructions.name: Prepare the vegetables
instructions.text: Put the cabbage, tomatoes, red onion and cooled, dry blanched bean sprouts in a wide bowl. If the onion tastes harsh, soak it in cold water for 5 minutes, drain and dry thoroughly before adding.

instructions.name: Mix the dressing
instructions.text: Whisk the fermented tea leaf dressing, lime juice, fish sauce, sugar and 3 tablespoons cooled garlic oil until glossy. Taste a small amount before adding salt because prepared lahpet and fish sauce vary widely in salinity.

instructions.name: Toss at the table
instructions.text: Add the dressing, half the crunchy mix and half the garlic chips to the vegetables. Toss for 30 seconds, pressing lightly with the spoon so the tea leaves disperse. Top with the remaining crunch and garlic. Serve immediately, with chile and hot rice offered separately.

why_it_works: Low, steady heat turns sliced garlic crisp before it burns and creates an aromatic oil that carries the tea leaf dressing through the cabbage.
Toasting peanuts, split peas, sesame and dried shrimp separately preserves the signature contrast between juicy vegetables and crunchy toppings.
Seeding tomatoes and drying sprouts prevent excess water from diluting the fermented tea, lime and fish sauce.
swaps: For a vegetarian version, omit dried shrimp and replace fish sauce with light soy sauce; check the prepared tea leaf dressing label for fish ingredients.
If roasted split peas are unavailable, use dry-roasted chickpeas or additional roasted peanuts for crunch.
Use finely shredded romaine plus 3 cups cabbage if you prefer a lighter texture, but avoid soft lettuces that wilt immediately.
storage: Store vegetables, dressing and crunchy toppings in three separate covered containers for up to 2 days. Keep sprouts at 40°F or below and discard any that smell sour or feel slimy. Once dressed, the salad is best eaten within 1 hour and should not be frozen. Refrigerate leftover rice within 2 hours and reheat to 165°F.
notes: Prepared fermented tea leaf dressing is sold chilled or jarred at many Southeast Asian markets and online; use a reputable commercial product and refrigerate it as labeled.
Fermented tea leaves contain caffeine. Portions vary by product, so people limiting caffeine should use less dressing or choose another salad.
Dried shrimp and fish sauce are salty; taste the mixed dressing before adding the optional salt.
Serve chile at the table to keep the shared salad mild.
This recipe contains peanuts, sesame, shellfish and fish; use the swaps and verify labels when cooking for allergies.

faqs.q: Can I ferment tea leaves at home for this salad?
faqs.a: This recipe intentionally uses prepared commercial lahpet. Safe fermentation requires controlled salt, acidity and sanitation; a jarred or refrigerated product gives a more dependable weeknight result.

faqs.q: Why did my garlic turn bitter?
faqs.a: It cooked too hot or stayed in the oil after becoming golden. Start garlic in cool oil, keep the heat medium-low and strain it while it is pale gold because carryover heat darkens it.

faqs.q: Can tea leaf salad be made ahead?
faqs.a: Prep the three components ahead, but toss only at serving time. Cabbage releases water, while peanuts, peas and garlic lose their crunch in the acidic dressing.

title: Dutch Stroopwafels with Cinnamon-Caramel Syrup
dek: Thin yeast waffles split while warm and sandwiched around buttery cinnamon caramel make a crisp-chewy café treat that softens over a hot mug.
image_alt: Thin round Dutch stroopwafel resting over a white mug of hot coffee
ingredients: 3/4 cup whole milk, warmed to 105 to 110°F
3/4 cup (170 g) unsalted butter, melted and cooled until warm
Nonstick spray or melted butter, for the waffle iron
1/3 cup light corn syrup or golden syrup

instructions.name: Wake the yeast
instructions.text: Stir the warm milk, yeast and granulated sugar in a small bowl. Let stand for 5 minutes, until lightly foamy. If the milk exceeds 115°F, let it cool before adding yeast.

instructions.name: Mix and proof the dough
instructions.text: Whisk the flour, salt and cinnamon in a large bowl. Add the yeast mixture, melted butter and egg and knead by hand or with a dough hook for 4 to 5 minutes, until smooth and soft. Cover and let rise in a warm place for 45 minutes; it will look puffy but may not double.

instructions.name: Cook the caramel syrup
instructions.text: Combine the brown sugar, butter, corn syrup, water, cinnamon and salt in a 2-quart saucepan over medium-low heat. Stir until melted, then simmer without vigorous boiling for 3 to 5 minutes, until smooth and 225 to 230°F. Remove from heat and stir in vanilla. Keep warm over the lowest heat; do not let it exceed 235°F or it will set too hard.

instructions.name: Portion and preheat
instructions.text: Divide the dough into 14 pieces of about 58 grams each and roll into balls. Preheat a shallow-grid stroopwafel iron, waffle-cone iron or pizzelle press according to its manual and grease lightly if the manufacturer recommends it.

instructions.name: Press the waffles
instructions.text: Place one dough ball in the center, close the iron and cook for 60 to 90 seconds, until evenly deep golden. Transfer to a board with a thin spatula. Keep uncooked dough covered and adjust timing for your iron; dark browning creates crispness, but black spots taste bitter.

instructions.name: Split while hot
instructions.text: Working immediately and wearing a heat-resistant glove on the hand holding the waffle, trim it to a 4-inch round if desired. Hold a thin serrated knife parallel to the board and carefully split the hot waffle into two thin discs. If it cools and resists, do not force it; use it as a single crisp waffle instead.

instructions.name: Fill and set
instructions.text: Spread about 1 tablespoon warm caramel nearly to the edge of one disc and top with the second, pressing gently. Repeat, returning the syrup to very low heat if it thickens. Cool the filled stroopwafels in a single layer for 30 minutes before stacking.

why_it_works: A soft, butter-rich yeast dough compresses into the characteristic thin grid while retaining enough structure to split when hot.
Holding the syrup below the hard-ball range keeps the filling chewy after cooling instead of turning brittle.
Splitting each waffle immediately uses steam and residual softness to create two delicate layers without baking a second wafer.
swaps: Golden syrup can replace light corn syrup one-for-one and gives the filling a slightly toastier flavor.
Use 2% milk in place of whole milk; avoid skim milk because the dough benefits from a little dairy fat.
If your pizzelle press makes 3-inch rounds, divide the dough into 20 pieces of about 40 grams and use roughly 2 teaspoons filling per cookie.
storage: Cool completely before storing airtight at room temperature for up to 7 days, separating layers with parchment. Rewarm one over a steaming mug for 1 to 2 minutes or in a 250°F oven for 3 minutes. Freeze airtight for up to 2 months and thaw at room temperature; do not microwave, which can make the caramel dangerously hot.
notes: Total time includes a 45-minute proof and a 30-minute cooling period; active work is about 65 minutes.
A standard deep Belgian waffle maker cannot press the wafers thin enough. Use a shallow-grid waffle-cone, pizzelle or dedicated stroopwafel iron.
Hot irons, wafers and caramel can burn. Use dry heat protection, keep fingers clear of the plates and split waffles on a stable board.
A digital scale keeps the wafers equal so they cook and split at the same rate.
Caramel temperature is a practical check, but appearance matters too: it should flow in a slow ribbon and remain spreadable on low heat.

faqs.q: Why do my stroopwafels crack when I split them?
faqs.a: They cooled too much, cooked too long or are too thick. Split each within about 20 seconds of opening the iron, use a gentle sawing motion and keep the remaining dough covered.

faqs.q: Why did the caramel become hard?
faqs.a: It cooked past about 235°F or boiled too long. Warm it gently with 1 tablespoon water; if it remains brittle, make a fresh batch and stop at 225 to 230°F.

faqs.q: Can I make the dough ahead?
faqs.a: Yes. After kneading, cover and refrigerate for up to 18 hours. Bring it toward room temperature for 30 minutes, portion and proceed; the cooler dough may need a few extra seconds in the iron.
